No skin is visible, so skin tone is null; age group adult per caption.

panels.figure_caption: Grayscale ultrasound image of a 57‐year‐old woman with a left breast mass. The lesion exhibits a hypoechoic echo pattern, non‐parallel orientation, irregular shape, spiculated margins, posterior acoustic shadowing, and a surrounding echogenic halo. Histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis confirmed a grade 1 invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) that is ER positive, PR positive, HER2 negative, with a Ki‐67 index of 6%.
in_text_mentions: Figures 1, 2, 3 illustrate ultrasound findings in three patients with breast masses, showcasing various sonographic features such as hypoechoic lesions, irregular shapes, non‐parallel orientation, spiculated or indistinct margins, posterior acoustic shadowing, and echogenic halos. These sonographic patterns were frequently observed in cases with specific histopathological and molecular features, as illustrated in Figures 1, 2, 3. This highlights the diagnostic utility of ultrasound imaging in evaluating breast lesions.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Sagittal DCE-MRI in a 38-year-old woman with biopsy-proven grade III invasive ductal carcinoma; panel shows an enhancing breast mass with irregular margins and central hypovascularity, consistent with the captioned malignancy. B: Axial delayed-phase DCE-MRI of the same invasive ductal carcinoma, showing the enhancing mass with central hypointensity; included as part of the same patient imaging. C: Diffusion-weighted image (b=700 s/mm2) of the known invasive ductal carcinoma, captioned as a hyperintense mass with a central hypointense component; no exact vocabulary finding key applies. D: ADC map from the same patient with invasive ductal carcinoma, showing a manually traced ROI and reported ADC value; included as a patient-specific diagnostic image, though no exact vocabulary finding key applies.

Correlation between apparent diffusion coefficient values in breast magnetic resonance imaging and prognostic factors of breast invasive ductal carcinoma.. Porto biomedical journal 2019. doi:10.1016/j.pbj.0000000000000027. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Thirty-eight-year-old woman with invasive ductal carcinoma in the upper external quadrant of the left breast. A, Sagittal dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging 2 minutes after contrast enhancement identified a round mass with subtle irregular margins. The lesion was characterized by peripheral enhancement with a small central hypovascular area. B, Axial dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging 10 minutes after contrast enhancement (delayed phase). C, On diffusion-weighted images acquired with a b value of 700 s/mm2, the tumor appeared as a hyperintense mass with a central hypointense component. D, A region of interest (ROI) within the margins of the lesion was manually traced on apparent diffusion coefficient maps, avoiding the central part. Apparent diffusion coefficient value was equal to 1.01 × 10–3 mm2/s. At histopathology, the lesion was defined as a grade III invasive ductal carcinoma. At the immunohistochemical analysis, hormonal receptor status was positive (estrogen and progesterone receptors), Ki67 expression was 60% and human epidermal growth factor receptor type 2 (HER2) status was equal to 0 (negative). Axillary lymph node status was negative.
in_text_mentions: The ROI was manually drawn in the slice in which the cancer presented a greater diameter (Fig. 1). Apparent necrotic or cystic components were avoided by referring to other MRIs. In cases with multifocal or multicentric masses the largest tumor was selected. The image analysis was performed by 2 radiologists with 2 and 20 years of experience on breast MRI. The final ADC value for each patient was obtained by consensus between the 2 radiologists, with the lowest being the preferred number.

in_text_mentions: specimen was sent for histopathological examination. During the processing of a specimen, a careful examination of the excised breast tissue revealed a 1.2 cm mass within a dilated duct, suspicious of intraductal carcinoma. The mass was located in close proximity to an area of prominent lymphocytic infiltration. The surrounding breast tissue showed evidence of chronic inflammation and fibrosis. panels.figure_caption: F-18 FDG whole body maximum intensity projection image and selected transaxial CT, PET and PET/CT fusion images of the breasts of a 58 year-old patient with right invasive ductal carcinoma who underwent right mastectomy and axillary dissection. Histopathology showed primary tumor in lower inner quadrant, 2.4×1.7×1.5 cm in size, with retroareolar extension and multiple microscopic foci (primary tumor grade 3, pathological stage T2N2A) as well as ductal carcinoma insitu surrounding the main tumor. PET showed the hypermetabolic primary tumor (SUVmax=12) (arrow) and multiple smaller hypermetabolic foci surrounding the primary tumor and also in retroareolar region (SUVmax=3.4, 3.7, 4.1 and 4.4) (short arrows) as well as right axillary lymph node metastases (SUVmax=8.9). Diffuse uptake is also seen in the skin of the right breast, indicating extension of the tumor

in_text_mentions: ectomy and axillary dissection, with written informed consent about the operative option from the patient. Postoperative pathological study showed cancer cells growing in solid and trabecular fashions, spreading in 25-mm sizes, with microvoids around cancer cell clusters, marked fat invasion, and two metastatic lymph nodes. Immunostaining of the tumor showed estrogen receptor positivity (Allred score 7), progesterone receptor negativity, human epidermal growth factor receptor type 2 equivocality (fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) negative), and a Ki-67 labeling index of 35% (Figure 4).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Craniocaudal mammographic view of the patient's biopsy-confirmed invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, showing an irregular iso-dense mass with obscured margins, matching the mammographic IDC finding vocabulary. B: Mediolateral oblique mammographic view of the same IDC-confirmed mass, showing the irregular iso-dense lesion described in the caption. C: Color Doppler ultrasound of the biopsy-proven invasive ductal carcinoma showing an irregular hypoechoic solid mass with indistinct margins and increased vascularity; the axillary lymphadenopathy finding is not applicable since the caption/in-text state no suspicious lymphadenopathy, so it is omitted. D: Maximum-intensity-projection dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI of the IDC-confirmed breast mass showing an enhancing irregular lesion with the adjacent vessel sign and prominent ipsilateral breast vascularity as stated in the caption.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: H-E stained section of the breast primary showing infiltrating solid nests/cords of pleomorphic tumor cells, explicitly captioned as invasive ductal carcinoma; article title and in-text (ER/PR/HER-2 negative, ypT3N3) confirm the target disease. Classic histologic appearance of IDC-NST. B: Endoscopic view of the ~1 cm elevated fundic lesion (white arrow) that proved to be a gastric metastasis of the patient's breast invasive ductal carcinoma; the article title explicitly attributes this gastric lesion to IDC of the breast, so the panel shows a disease manifestation (metastatic spread) rather than a separate primary gastric cancer. No IDC-specific endoscopic finding exists in the vocabulary, hence proposed finding; typicality variant as gastric metastasis is an uncommon site.
